# RESY

<!-- badges: start -->
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
[![CRAN status](https://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/RESY)](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=RESY)
<!-- badges: end -->

RESY assigns vegetation plots to vegetation or habitat types based on their
plant community. A plot where beech, silver fir and beech-forest herbs such as
wood sorrel grow together is a beech-fir montane forest. A plot where mat-grass
(*Nardus stricta*) is abundant is an acidic grassland. RESY uses the species
composition and cover or abundance recorded in each vegetation plot (relevé).

The rules for this assignment form an expert system (ESy; Chytrý et al.
[2020](https://doi.org/10.1111/avsc.12519); Bruelheide et al.
[2021](https://doi.org/10.1111/avsc.12562)), stored as a text or JSON file. For
each type, the rule specifies which groups of indicator species a plot must
contain and how much cover they must have. In the example below, a plot is a
beech-fir montane forest when beech and silver fir together cover more than 15%
of it and beech-forest herbs more than 10%. You can also supply your own expert
system.

RESY ships the expert system for EUNIS (European Nature Information System), the
habitat classification of the
[European Environment Agency](https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/datahub/datahubitem-view/123d0c9a-a6fa-4f2d-b887-5d8e5468faed)
for the land and sea of Europe. EUNIS defines a habitat by its plant and animal
communities together with abiotic conditions. Some of its rules therefore also
use site data, such as the ecoregion, the country or the position on the coast.

The EUNIS expert system uses the species names of
[Euro+Med PlantBase](https://europlusmed.org/), the taxonomy used in data from
the [European Vegetation Archive (EVA)](https://euroveg.org/eva-database/). Species names
in plot data that follow another taxonomy, such as [GBIF](https://www.gbif.org/)
or [World Flora Online](https://www.worldfloraonline.org/), must first be
matched to Euro+Med names. Use `resy_resolve_taxa()` to match them
(`vignette("taxonomy")`).

## :arrow_double_down: Installation

The package is available on CRAN. Install and load it with:

``` r
install.packages("RESY")
library("RESY")
```

RESY is still under active development. You can install the development
version from the GitHub repository using the following commands:

``` r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github(
   "https://github.com/florian-jansen/resy",
   dependencies = TRUE
   )
library(RESY)
```

## :rocket: Usage

To classify plots, `resy_classify()` needs two tables:

- A **species table**, with one row per species in each plot, giving the plot
  ID, species name and cover.
- A **header table**, with one row per plot, giving the plot ID and any site
  data used by the classification rules.

This example uses the bundled plots from Tuscany and `Apennine-test`, a small
expert system whose rules require no site data. The header table therefore
contains only plot IDs, but `resy_classify()` still requires it.

```{r usage, message = FALSE}
library(RESY)

file <- system.file("extdata", "data_example_species.csv", package = "RESY")
species <- read.csv(file)
header <- unique(species["PlotObservationID"])

res <- resy_classify(species, header, scheme = "Apennine-test")
cand <- resy_candidates(res, top_n = 3, wide = TRUE)
table(cand$classification)
```

`F`, `FB`, `N`, `NG` and `NS` are the five vegetation types of `Apennine-test`.
A plot marked `?` meets no type's rule and is not classified. Here, 92 of the
200 plots remain unclassified. In these plots, all four indicator groups have at
most 4% cover, below the lowest threshold in the rules (5%).

Each type has a priority in the expert system. When a plot meets the rules of
several types, it is assigned to the one with the highest priority. Each row of
`cand` is one plot: the type it is assigned to, then the types whose rules it
meets, highest priority first. Plot `CX45` meets the rules of `FB` (beech-fir
montane forest, priority 5) and of its parent type `F` (forest, priority 2), and
is assigned to `FB`:

```{r usage-candidates}
cand[cand$plot_id == "CX45", ]
```

`resy_eval_plot(res, p = "CX45")` shows the species and conditions behind this
assignment. For EUNIS, the header table also needs site data such as the
ecoregion and the country, which `resy_harmonize_eunis()` adds from the plot
coordinates.

Column names can follow [Darwin Core](https://dwc.tdwg.org/), a standard set of
field names for biodiversity data. The example data stores species names in
`scientificName`. RESY looks for the species in `TaxonName` or `scientificName`
(any other column is set with `species_col`), the plot ID in `eventID`, the cover
in `organismQuantity` with an `organismQuantityType` of `"% cover"`, and the site
data in `decimalLongitude`, `decimalLatitude`, `country`,
`minimumElevationInMeters` and `maximumElevationInMeters`.

## :scroll: Vignettes

We have written several vignettes to help you use the RESY R package:
<br>

- `vignette("RESY")`: start here, from a species table to classified plots
- `vignette("EUNIS")`: EUNIS habitat types for plots with coordinates
- `vignette("altitude-vignette")`: the altitude column some EUNIS rules use
- `vignette("taxonomy")`: matching the species names in your data to the
  names the expert system uses

## :desktop_computer: Functions

These are the main functions:

- `resy_harmonize_eunis()` adds the site data EUNIS needs (ecoregion, country,
  coast, dunes) from the plot coordinates.
- `resy_check_taxonomy()` checks which species names the expert system knows;
  `resy_resolve_taxa()` matches names from other taxonomies to them.
- `resy_classify()` assigns each plot to a vegetation or habitat type.
- `resy_candidates()` lists the assigned and candidate types per plot.
- `resy_eval_plot()` explains the assignment of one plot.
- `resy_validate_esy()` checks your own expert system, and
  `resy_add_classification()` makes it available to `resy_classify()`.

An overview of all functions and data is given in the tab
[**Reference**](https://florian-jansen.github.io/resy/reference/).

## :books: Papers and links

- Bruelheide et al. ([2021](https://doi.org/10.1111/avsc.12562)): the
  expert-system language that RESY implements.
- Chytrý et al. ([2020](https://doi.org/10.1111/avsc.12519)): the EUNIS expert
  system, its species groups and the habitat distribution maps.
- [EUNIS-ESy on Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/16895007): the released
  versions of the EUNIS expert system.
- [FloraVeg.EU](https://floraveg.eu/habitat/): descriptions of every EUNIS
  habitat type.

## :memo: How to cite

```{r citation, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cit <- citation("RESY")
fence <- function(lang, x) {
  cat("```", lang, "\n", paste(x, collapse = "\n\n"), "\n```\n\n", sep = "")
}
cat(attr(cit, "mheader"), "\n\n", sep = "")
fence("text", format(cit, style = "text"))
cat("BibTeX:\n\n")
fence("bibtex", format(cit, style = "bibtex"))
```
